slides: Critical thinking.
The last row of the content rubric. And the one that covers everything.
It has four parts. A precise definition of the issue, opinion versus fact, several perspectives, and dealing with opposing views. Let's take them one by one.
A precise definition of the issue. We already talked about it, it's relevance to the task. But let's look at some examples.
Now, the students in these examples don't miss completely. They don't start writing about horse racing. They land next to the issue.
And next to it isn't good enough. If you miss what you were asked, it's as if you wrote an essay on a different topic.
Officially, content that doesn't relate to the task gets the lowest score. And 'little relevance' is at the very bottom of the table. So this is critical.
Example one.
Custody means who the child lives with, on which days, and so on. Until age six, the child is with the mother. Only then do they start talking about shared custody.
So what do you say? This misses the issue.
The issue is the tender years presumption. But the student started discussing whether a court should decide at all, or psychologists. That's next to the issue, not the issue.
Another example.
The question is about limiting the number of weekly flights. The answer talks about the environment in general, and about recycling. Not about flights.
By the way, there's another way to miss this task. Arguing for limiting flights for some other reason, not the damage to the ozone layer. It seems to answer the question, but it misses the task.
So always check. What exactly is being decided, who it affects, and which conditions the question sets.
Opinion versus fact. This is one of the main problems in students' essays. A lot of them present their opinions as facts.
Picture a line, from not true, to true.
A fact is true for sure. It sits at the true end.
And an opinion? Well, I don't know where it sits. Maybe it's true, maybe it isn't. I can't decide. I'd need experiments, research.
If you ask a lot of people, some will say yes, and some will say no.
And by the way, exam tasks are chosen so that the opinions on each side are around fifty-fifty.
If almost everyone agreed with one side, or if it were a fact, there'd be nothing to discuss. The task would be useless.
They want to see how we argue. How we build arguments, and develop them. A question about a fact doesn't do that.
So your position will always be an opinion. What matters is what you build it from.
Now, between opinion and fact there's another idea. A reasonable assumption.
It's not a fact. I didn't go and check it. But I can say, it's reasonable to assume that...
For example. It's reasonable to assume that criminals who know an area is monitored will avoid committing crimes there.
It's not a fact. Maybe there's a criminal who doesn't care about the cameras. But the reasonable person would probably act this way.
A fact is really powerful, because it's true. And a reasonable assumption is more powerful than an opinion.

When I develop an argument, I rely on steps. Links, mini-arguments. We'll call them the chain, the cause-and-effect steps, and they get their own lesson later. The ideal is to build them from facts and reasonable assumptions.
Now, if my whole development is... I think this causes that, I think that causes this, I think this causes that, and here's the result...
That's very weak. It's hard to convince anyone. Someone else just says, I think it won't. And that won't either. And that won't either.
But if I use facts and reasonable assumptions more than opinions, I make the argument, and its development, stronger.
Say my argument is an opinion. Installing cameras in public spaces will reduce crime. So how do I explain it with facts and reasonable assumptions?
Fact. The cameras will be installed with the public's knowledge. Not secretly.
Reasonable assumption. People who know there are cameras will probably avoid crime in those areas.
And I can make it stronger with a comparison. Similarly to speed cameras on the roads.

Some speed cameras are even on brightly painted poles, so we won't miss them. Why? Because their goal is less to catch drivers, and more to deter them. When we know a camera is there, we drive slower.
And I don't need to repeat the explanation in other words. That would be repetition and padding. The comparison says it for me.
Another reason, same method.
Fact. Enforcement agencies will be able to use the footage. Well, obviously, that's why we build the database.
So it's reasonable to assume it'll be easier to identify offenders. Compare that to asking witnesses... 'He wore a hat... maybe an eye patch?'
Conclusion, crime goes down? Wait. My argument isn't full yet. I caught him after the fact. Why would that reduce crime?
So I complete it. It'll be easier to prove their guilt. So they'll go to prison instead of being released. So crime goes down.
My argument was an opinion. But I built its development from facts and reasonable assumptions, and that makes it much stronger. This is the chain, with every step tested.
Looking at the issue from several perspectives.
We'll have a whole lesson on looking at an issue from different areas. Social, educational, economic, the rights involved.
And lessons on finding arguments. From the task, who is involved, and points of view.
When I look at the issue from several perspectives, it shows more impressive critical thinking than someone who looks very, very narrowly.
And dealing with opposing views.
Remember, there's no right and wrong here. There are different positions, and both are legitimate.
Know the advantages of your position. But also its disadvantages, so you can deal with them if they come up.
And know the other side's advantages and disadvantages, so you can weaken their counter-arguments.
Later we'll learn the recommended essay structure. It has a rebuttal paragraph. We present an opposing argument, weaken it, and answer it.
That shows we took the counter-arguments into account, and we have a way to deal with them.
And this matters a lot to the raters. Without dealing with the opposing view, the score may be medium... but it's very hard for it to be high.
